content: There is a concern that maternal HIV or AIDS may be incorrectly assigned as the cause of death in all perinatal deaths where the mother is HIV-positive, even in the absence of evidence supporting this as the cause. While maternal HIV can increase the risk of perinatal death, establishing a direct causal relationship is often challenging. It is important to differentiate perinatal deaths that occur in the context of other maternal conditions where HIV is incidental. Classifying each case based on maternal HIV status is preferable, as it provides a clearer understanding of the role of maternal HIV and AIDS in perinatal deaths. Case 1: A 19-year-old woman, para 1, at 38 weeks of gestation, presented in good health during labor with no significant medical history. She delivered a 2450 g baby after 8 hours of labor. The baby died on the second day of life due to meconium aspiration syndrome. Clinical review identified modifiable factors, including undetected fetal distress during labor and insufficiently experienced personnel managing the case. The neonatal cause of death was meconium aspiration syndrome, and no maternal condition was identified at the time of perinatal death. The death occurred in the neonatal period. This case highlights the importance of identifying no maternal condition as a maternal code during perinatal death and emphasizes the need for continued training in intrapartum care and obstetric emergencies. Case 2: A 30-year-old woman, para 1, at 39 weeks of gestation, presented in labor with a live fetus. She was HIV-positive and on long-term antiretroviral therapy. Labor progress was poor due to incorrect interpretation of the partograph. An acute intrapartum event led to a hypoxic stillbirth. The fetus was delivered via cesarean section. The intrapartum cause of death was intrapartum hypoxia, and the maternal condition was obstructed labor. This case underscores the need to capture maternal conditions beyond HIV. Case 3: A 16-year-old woman, para 0, with no medical history, presented in spontaneous labor at 29 weeks of gestation. She delivered a live baby weighing 1100 g via forceps delivery. The baby died on the second day of life due to hyaline membrane disease. The neonatal cause of death was hyaline membrane disease, and the maternal condition was spontaneous preterm labor. This case highlights the need to identify specific causes of neonatal premature death beyond prematurity. Additionally, spontaneous preterm labor, despite the absence of maternal medical history, should be recorded as the main maternal condition contributing to the perinatal death. Case 4: A 36-year-old woman, para 5, at 35 weeks of gestation, presented with complaints of headache and decreased fetal movements. Intrauterine fetal death was diagnosed. Clinical and biochemical investigations revealed maternal proteinuric hypertension. Spontaneous vaginal delivery of a macerated stillborn weighing 2100 g followed labor induction. The proteinuric hypertension resolved subsequently. The antepartum cause of death was intrauterine hypoxia, and the maternal condition was pre-eclampsia. This case highlights the importance of always capturing the maternal condition, as the fetal cause of death (intrauterine hypoxia) provides less specific information compared to the maternal condition (pre-eclampsia). The WHO application of ICD-10 to perinatal deaths (ICD-PM) aims to improve the classification of perinatal deaths and establish clearer linkages to maternal conditions. This system enables health workers to certify perinatal deaths with greater clarity and supports public health interventions that address the needs of both mother and baby. The ICD-PM builds on the ICD-10 framework and incorporates new concepts such as the timing of perinatal death and mandatory linkage to maternal conditions. Further research and monitoring of its application are necessary to optimize its use.
